items.abstract: <jats:p>Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are no longer a research curiosity-they are being deployed in production environments across industries. Yet for all the progress in what these systems can do, comparatively little attention has been paid to how, and under what conditions, they break. This paper attempts to fill part of that gap. Drawing on over forty published works from 2020 through early 2025, I propose a four-dimensional taxonomy of LLM agent failure modes, organized around the core functional modules present in most agentic architectures: reasoning and planning, tool use and action execution, memory and context management, and multi-agent orchestration. For each dimension, I provide formal definitions of specific failure classes, describe triggering conditions, and supply concrete illustrative examples grounded in the empirical literature. I also introduce the Agent Robustness Evaluation Protocol (AREP)-a lightweight, framework-agnostic robustness evaluation methodology intended to surface latent failure risks before deployment rather than after. The paper concludes with seven practitioner recommendations for building agentic systems that are not merely capable, but meaningfully robust and reliable.</jats:p>
title: Why AI Agents Fail: A Taxonomy of Failure Modes in Autonomous LLM-Based Systems

items.abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents serve as proxies for human investors in behavioral finance experiments? I deploy 96 GPT-4-family agents in a staggered difference-in-differences design, exposing treated agents to exogenous attention shocks and viral social media signals about meme stocks while holding the fundamentals constant. Whereas human retail investors substantially increase net purchases of attention-grabbing stocks, LLM agents reduce buying propensity by 11.67 percentage points (SE = 4.92, p = .018), equivalent to preventing one purchase for every 8.6 treated agent-period observations. The direction and magnitude of this effect are robust across all specifications, although conservative small-sample variance corrections widen the confidence interval. Agents also display a reversed disposition effect, selling losers 3:1 relative to winners, directly contradicting the human pattern driven by loss aversion. To explain these divergences, I develop the Normative-Descriptive Divergence (NDD) model, formalizing how prescriptive training corpora ('avoid hype,' 'cut losses') generate systematic departures from the emotion-driven behavior observed in human investors. Even when explicitly prompted to exhibit FOMO, agents rationally retreat when attention shocks impose calculable costs, revealing a strict constraint hierarchy in which quantitative optimization overrides persona-level instructions. These findings establish boundary conditions for “Homo Silicus” research: LLMs approximate normative economic benchmarks but fail to replicate biases rooted in emotional processing.
title: Homo Silicus is Hyper-Rational:  Why LLM Agents Fail to Replicate Attention-Driven Trading

items.abstract: <jats:p>India's digital narrative centers on the expansion of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), yet a systemic technical friction point remains: the lack of Universal Acceptance (UA). This paper examines the failure of prominent Indian e-commerce applications to support Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs) and Email Address Internationalization (EAI), focusing on the .bharat TLD. Through empirical testing of five dominant retail platforms, this study identifies antiquated validation protocols and backend infrastructure gaps as the primary drivers of digital exclusion for non-English speaking demographics.</jats:p>
title: Evaluating UA-Readiness in Indian E-commerce Apps: Why .bharat Email Addresses Still Fail in 2026
